analogy.p: Think of particles as people. In a solid they are like fans seated in fixed seats at a stadium: packed tightly, regular rows, only wriggling in place. In a liquid they are like a packed crowd that can shuffle past each other. In a gas they are like a few people in a huge open field, running about in random directions. Density is the number of people (mass) per area of space: the stadium and the crowd are dense, the field is not. The analogy breaks down because real particles attract and repel each other and are far smaller and numerous.
analogy.t: A car park and a crowded bus

bullets: Know the **arrangement, movement and forces** between particles in each state.
Recall and use **density = mass / volume** (ρ = m / V), in kg/m³ and g/cm³.
Explain **why gases are far less dense** than solids and liquids.
Describe how to find **volume** of a regular object (by measuring dimensions) and an irregular object (by displacement of water).
Describe how to find the **density of a liquid** using a measuring cylinder and balance.
Evaluate the method: **sources of error, ways to improve accuracy**, and use a graph of mass against volume.
Know that **mass is conserved** when a substance changes state, because the number of particles stays the same.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know and do
core.p: AQA 4.3.1 requires you to use the **particle model** to explain the differences between solids, liquids and gases, to recall and use the equation **density = mass / volume**, and to explain why density differs between the states of matter. You must also carry out and understand **Required Practical 17**: investigating the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids. Marks are earned for correct method, correct use of equipment, accurate calculations with units, and for explaining sources of error.

bullets: **Arrangement:** regular, closely packed, in a fixed pattern.
**Movement:** vibrate about fixed positions; the more energy (the hotter), the **larger the vibrations**.
**Forces:** strong forces of attraction hold particles in place.
**Properties:** fixed shape, fixed volume, cannot flow, very difficult to compress.
**Density:** generally high, because particles are closely packed.
**Why they keep their shape:** particles cannot slide past each other as the forces between them are too strong.
Heating a solid increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles, so vibrations increase; most solids expand slightly.
core.p: In the particle model, all matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules or ions). In a **solid**, the particles are held in fixed positions by **strong forces of attraction** between them. They are arranged in a **regular pattern (lattice)** and are very close together, touching their neighbours. The particles cannot move from place to place, but they **vibrate about fixed positions**. This explains why solids have a **fixed shape and fixed volume** and cannot easily be compressed.

bullets: **Arrangement:** random, close together (touching).
**Movement:** particles move around and slide past one another.
**Forces:** weaker than in solids but still significant (not negligible).
**Properties:** no fixed shape (takes the shape of its container), fixed volume, flows, almost incompressible.
**Density:** similar to the solid form of the same substance (usually slightly lower).
**Evaporation** happens at the surface when fast-moving particles have enough energy to escape the attraction of neighbouring particles.
As temperature rises, the average **speed of the particles** increases.
core.p: In a **liquid**, the particles are still close together and in contact with one another, but they are arranged **randomly** rather than in a pattern. The forces of attraction are weaker than in a solid, so the particles are able to **move past each other**, sliding and tumbling over one another. This explains why liquids **flow** and take the shape of their container, but have a **fixed volume** and are very difficult to compress because the particles are already touching.

bullets: **Arrangement:** random, very widely spaced.
**Movement:** fast, random, in straight lines between collisions.
**Forces:** negligible between particles.
**Properties:** fills its container, no fixed shape or volume, easily compressed, flows.
**Density:** very low (about 1000 times smaller than a solid or liquid at normal conditions), because the same number of particles occupies a much larger volume.
**Pressure:** caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container (covered in 4.3.3).
In particle diagrams for a gas, show **few particles, large gaps, no pattern**.
core.p: In a **gas**, the particles are **far apart** compared with their size, and there is almost nothing between them. The forces of attraction between particles are **negligible (almost zero)**, so particles move **rapidly in random directions** in straight lines until they collide with other particles or the walls of the container. Because of this, gases have **no fixed shape or volume**: they spread out to fill any container, and they can be compressed easily because there is so much empty space.

bullets: **Equation:** density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) ÷ volume (m³), written ρ = m / V.
**Rearrangements:** m = ρ × V and V = m ÷ ρ. Use the formula triangle if helpful: m on top, ρ and V underneath.
**Units:** kg/m³ when mass is in kg and volume in m³; g/cm³ when mass is in g and volume in cm³.
**Conversion:** 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (so water, 1 g/cm³, is 1000 kg/m³).
**Volume conversion:** 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 cm³ = 1 ml; 1 litre = 1000 cm³.
**Meaning:** a density of 1000 kg/m³ means 1 m³ of the material has a mass of 1000 kg.
**Float or sink:** an object floats in a fluid if it is **less dense** than that fluid, and sinks if it is **more dense**.
core.p: **Density** is a measure of **how much mass is packed into a given volume**. A dense material has a lot of mass in a small space; a low-density material has little mass in the same space. It is calculated using **density = mass ÷ volume**. The symbol for density is ρ (the Greek letter rho). Density is a property of the **material**, not of the size of the object: a small iron nail and a large iron block have the same density, even though their masses are different.

bullets: **Water:** about 1000 kg/m³ (1.0 g/cm³).
**Ice:** about 920 kg/m³, slightly less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.
**Air:** about 1.2 kg/m³ at room temperature.
**Aluminium:** about 2700 kg/m³ (2.7 g/cm³).
**Iron:** about 7900 kg/m³ (7.9 g/cm³).
**Gold:** about 19 300 kg/m³; **lead** about 11 300 kg/m³.
Values in the exam are usually given in the question; you do not need to memorise them exactly, but you should know **water = 1 g/cm³**.
core.p: It helps to know the approximate densities of some common materials, so you can check that your answers are sensible. Most solids and liquids are of the order of 1000 to 10 000 kg/m³, whereas gases are around 1 kg/m³. A calculated density far outside these ranges, such as 0.002 kg/m³ for a metal, usually shows a unit error or a calculation slip.

bullets: Solid → liquid: particles stay close, so the volume changes only a little; density changes only slightly.
Liquid → gas: particles move far apart, so volume increases enormously and **density drops sharply**.
**Water is an exception:** ice is less dense than liquid water, because in ice the particles are held in an open lattice with gaps.
Heating a substance normally makes it **expand**, so density decreases slightly as temperature rises (the mass is constant but the volume rises).
In a gas, compressing it forces particles closer together, so the **density increases** while the mass remains the same.
Always link the answer to **particle spacing** when explaining a difference in density.
core.p: Density depends on how many particles of a given mass are packed into a given volume. When a substance changes state, the **mass stays the same** but the **volume changes** because the spacing between particles changes. In a solid and a liquid, particles are touching, so their densities are similar. In a gas, the particles are far apart, so the same mass occupies a far greater volume and the density is much lower.

bullets: **Mass is conserved** in a change of state because the number of particles does not change.
The **volume and density** may change, even though the mass does not.
Changes of state: melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), boiling/evaporation (liquid → gas), condensing (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas).
**Physical change** = no new substances made, reversible; **chemical change** = new substances made.
During a change of state the **internal energy** changes, as energy is used to break or form forces between particles (covered in 4.3.2).
Exam link: if asked 'what happens to the mass when ice melts?', the answer is **it stays the same** because particles are not lost.
core.h: Conservation of mass and changes of state
core.p: When a substance melts, freezes, boils, evaporates, condenses or sublimes, the change is a **physical change**, not a chemical change. The particles stay the same; only their arrangement and energy change. As a result, **mass is conserved**: the mass before the change equals the mass after. A physical change is **reversible**: the substance can return to its original state and recover its original properties.

bullets: **Apparatus:** electronic balance, ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers, measuring cylinders, eureka (displacement) can, beakers, string or thread.
**Regular solid** (cube, cuboid, cylinder): volume calculated from measured dimensions.
**Irregular solid** (stone, key): volume found by **displacement of water**.
**Liquid:** volume read from a measuring cylinder; mass found by weighing.
**Aim:** to determine the density of each sample and compare with accepted values.
**Variables:** independent = the sample used; dependent = its density (calculated). Control: temperature, same balance, zeroed correctly.
**Repeat** each measurement and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
core.p: The required practical asks you to find the density of three types of sample: **regular solids**, **irregular solids** and **liquids**. In every case you need the **mass** (using a balance) and the **volume**, then you calculate density using ρ = m / V. How you find the volume is what changes. The practical is all about careful, accurate measurements, and the exam tests the method, errors and analysis.

bullets: 1. Place the object on the **electronic balance** (after zeroing) and record the **mass in g**.
2. Measure the **length, width and height** (or diameter and length for a cylinder) with a ruler or callipers; record in cm.
3. Calculate volume: **cuboid V = l × w × h**; **cylinder V = π × r² × h**, where r = diameter ÷ 2; **sphere V = 4/3 × π × r³** (if needed).
4. Calculate density using **ρ = m ÷ V** (g/cm³).
5. Repeat with other samples or measure each dimension several times and calculate a **mean**.
6. Convert to kg/m³ by multiplying by 1000 if required.
Reduce errors by measuring at several points and using equipment with a smaller resolution (for example micrometer for thickness).
core.h: Method: density of a regular solid
core.p: For a regular solid, you find the mass on a balance and then measure the lengths needed to calculate the volume. Choose equipment with suitable **resolution**: Vernier callipers or a micrometer give smaller uncertainties than a ruler, especially for small objects. Take several readings at different places on the object and take a mean, since the object may not be perfectly uniform.

bullets: 1. Measure the **mass** of the object on the balance.
2. Fill the **eureka can** with water until it just overflows from the spout; wait for dripping to stop; place an empty **measuring cylinder** under the spout.
3. Lower the object **slowly and carefully** into the can using thread so that it is completely submerged and does not splash.
4. Collect all the displaced water in the measuring cylinder and record the **volume (cm³)** with the eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
5. Calculate **ρ = m ÷ V**.
**Alternative method:** put water in a measuring cylinder, record the volume, lower the object in and record the new volume; **volume of object = final − initial**.
The object must be **completely submerged**, must **not float** (use a sinker if needed) and must not **absorb water**.
core.h: Method: density of an irregular solid (displacement)
core.p: A stone has no simple dimensions, so its volume cannot be calculated from measurements. Instead you use the fact that an object **displaces its own volume** of water when fully submerged. You can use a **eureka can**: fill the can until water just runs out of the spout, then lower the object in on thread and collect the water that overflows in a measuring cylinder. The volume of water collected equals the volume of the object.

bullets: 1. Place an empty **measuring cylinder** on the balance and record its mass, **m₁** (or zero the balance with it on).
2. Pour in some of the liquid; read the **volume V** with your eye level with the **bottom of the meniscus**.
3. Place the cylinder with liquid on the balance and record the mass **m₂**.
4. Mass of liquid = **m₂ − m₁**.
5. Calculate **density = (m₂ − m₁) ÷ V**.
6. Repeat with different volumes; plot a graph and find the gradient, or take a mean of the densities.
Reduce error: use a smaller measuring cylinder for a smaller volume to improve resolution, and read the scale at eye level.
core.p: To find the density of a liquid, you need the **mass of a known volume** of the liquid. You use a measuring cylinder to measure the volume and a balance to find the mass of the liquid by taking away the mass of the empty container. This is called finding mass by difference.

bullets: **Air bubbles** trapped on an irregular object increase the apparent volume; remove them by tapping.
**Parallax error** when reading volumes: view the meniscus from the side at eye level.
**Splashing** when lowering an object into water loses water, giving too small a volume.
**Not zeroing the balance** introduces a systematic error in mass.
**Low resolution** of equipment: a ruler (1 mm) is less precise than callipers (0.1 mm or 0.01 mm).
**Porous materials** absorb water, giving a false volume.
**Repeat readings** and take a mean to reduce the effect of random errors.
**Percentage uncertainty** is larger for small objects; use the largest sample possible within the equipment.
core.p: Marks are given for identifying **sources of error** and suggesting **improvements**. Random errors cause readings to vary and are reduced by repeating and taking a mean. Systematic errors, such as a balance that does not read zero, shift all results in the same direction and are reduced by checking and zeroing equipment before measuring. Resolution (the smallest division on the equipment) limits how precisely you can measure.

bullets: **Gradient** = change in mass ÷ change in volume = density.
A line **through the origin** shows density is constant (mass is directly proportional to volume).
A steeper line means a **higher density**.
**Safety:** wipe up spilt water to avoid slipping; do not drop heavy objects on feet or the balance; handle glassware with care.
**Link:** floating and sinking depend on comparing density of the object with the fluid.
**Link:** pressure in a fluid depends on density (Higher/extension), and gas density changes with pressure and temperature.
**Link to Chemistry:** the particle model explains melting, boiling and diffusion.
core.h: Graphs, safety and links to other topics
core.p: An excellent way to present results is to plot **mass (y-axis) against volume (x-axis)** for several samples of the same material. A material of constant density gives a **straight line through the origin**, and the **gradient equals the density**. Safety is also assessed: this practical is low risk, but you should note hazards and a sensible control. The idea of particles and density links to pressure in fluids, floating and sinking, and the chemistry of states of matter.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe' = give a step-by-step method; 'explain' = give reasons using particles; 'calculate' = use the equation, show working and units.
**1 mark:** write the equation density = mass ÷ volume or state that gases have widely spaced particles.
**2 marks:** state a property of a state and link to the particles, for example 'a gas can be compressed (1) because there is a lot of space between the particles (1)'.
**3-4 marks (method):** list the apparatus, what is measured, how volume is found and how density is calculated, in the correct order.
**6 marks (practical):** give a full method with measurements, repeats, mean, calculation, and at least one error or precaution; a logical order is essential.
**Calculation marks:** substitution (1), correct rearrangement/answer (1), unit (1). Always show working and convert units before substituting.
**Model phrases:** 'volume is found by displacement of water', 'read the volume at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus', 'repeat and calculate a mean', 'zero the balance before measuring'.
**Graph tip:** mass (y) against volume (x), line of best fit through the origin; **gradient = density**; draw a large gradient triangle.
**Conversions:** 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³; 1 cm³ = 1 ml; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
**Evaluation:** mention resolution of equipment, air bubbles, parallax error, and say how to reduce each.

mistakes.r: Density is **mass per unit volume** (ρ = m / V); it is not the same as mass or weight.
mistakes.w: Density is the weight of something.

mistakes.r: Particles in a gas are **far apart**, so the same mass is spread over a much larger volume.
mistakes.w: Gases are less dense because the particles are lighter.

mistakes.r: Particles in a solid **vibrate about fixed positions**.
mistakes.w: The particles in a solid do not move.

mistakes.r: Particles in a liquid are **close together and touching**, but randomly arranged and able to move past each other.
mistakes.w: The particles in a liquid are far apart.

mistakes.r: Keep units consistent: **g with cm³** gives g/cm³; **kg with m³** gives kg/m³.
mistakes.w: Using cm³ for volume with kg for mass.

mistakes.r: Read at **eye level** from the **bottom of the meniscus** to avoid parallax error.
mistakes.w: Read the measuring cylinder from above.

mistakes.r: **Mass is conserved** because the number of particles does not change.
mistakes.w: Mass changes when a substance melts or boils.

mistakes.r: Volume of the stone = the volume of water **displaced** (collected), or **final reading − initial reading**.
mistakes.w: Volume of a stone = water in the can.

summary: The specification asks you to use the particle model to explain the arrangement, movement and forces in solids, liquids and gases, to use density = mass / volume, and to carry out the required practical to find the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids. It matters because density explains floating, sinking and the huge difference between gases and solids or liquids.

terms.d: A model in which matter is made of tiny moving particles, used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
The mass of a substance per unit volume; density = mass ÷ volume.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg) or grams (g).
The amount of space an object occupies, measured in m³ or cm³.
The volume of water pushed aside when an object is fully submerged, equal to the volume of the object.
A container with a spout used to collect the water displaced by a submerged object.
The curved upper surface of a liquid in a container; read at the bottom of the curve at eye level.
The smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can detect.
An error in reading a scale caused by viewing it from the wrong angle.
An unpredictable variation in measurements, reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
An error that shifts all readings in the same direction, for example a balance that is not zeroed.
The regular, repeating arrangement of particles in a solid.
Able to be squeezed into a smaller volume; true of gases but not of solids or liquids.
A change, such as a change of state, in which no new substance is formed and which can be reversed.
Mass is neither created nor destroyed; the mass before and after a change of state is the same.
A device for measuring small lengths very precisely, often to 0.01 mm.
An instrument for measuring lengths, such as diameters, with a resolution of about 0.1 mm or better.

worked.q: A metal cube has sides of 5.0 cm and a mass of 337.5 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³. (3 marks)

worked.ans: 9.75 g/cm³ (or 9750 kg/m³); displacement gives the volume of an irregular object.
worked.q: A stone has a mass of 195 g. When placed in a measuring cylinder, the water level rises from 50 cm³ to 70 cm³. Calculate the density and explain why this method is used. (4 marks)
steps: Explanation: the stone is irregular, so its volume cannot be calculated from dimensions; it displaces its own volume of water.
